ENCHANTED ROCK, LLC'S COMMENTS REGARDING PROPOSED NEW RULE 16
      TAC § 25.521, LARGE LOAD DEMAND MANAGEMENT SERVICE

       Enchanted Rock, LLC ("ERock") appreciates the careful consideration being given to
establish the service for large load demand management under PURA §39.170(b).
       ERock is a Houston-based microgrid owner, operator, and developer with over 350 dual-
purpose microgrids in operation throughout Texas, providing over 560 MW of gas-fired,
dispatchable capacity to the grid. ERock is also operational in states across the country in support
of critical facilities and large loads. ERock does not have specific comments in response to the
questions posed in the Proposal for Publication ("PFP") but respectfully encourages the Public
Utility Commission of Texas ("Commission") to consider the following general comments as it
relates to the development of the Large Load Demand Management Service ("LLDMS").


GENERAL COMMENTS
       ERock appreciates the Commission' s efforts to implement the LLDMS required by Senate
Bill 6 ("SB 6"). Large loads can provide substantial reliability value to the ERCOT system,
particularly when paired with flexible, dispatchable onsite generation and storage. However,
ERock is concerned that, as drafted, the proposed construct is unlikely to generate meaningful
participation from the customers and resources best positioned to provide that value.
        The proposed as-needed procurement construct does not provide the certainty necessary to
support meaningful participation or investment. Previous comments from ERock in this
proceeding noted that short duration and ad hoc demand response procurements have historically
struggled to attract firm resources because they provide insufficient lead time and investment
certainty.1 Large data centers, manufacturing facilities, and other firm loads generally face
significant operational costs associated with curtailing their underlying operations. For these



1 April 8,2026 ERock Comments: https://interchange.puc.texas.gov/Documents/58482 20 1618447.PDF

                                              Page 1 of 5
 customers, an uncertain opportunity to receive compensation during an infrequent extreme weather
event is unlikely to justify either routine operational curtailment or investment in the generation,
storage, controls, and other infrastructure necessary to provide dependable flexibility.
        Recent analysis of the economics of AI computing further illustrates this challenge. Hans
Royal' s Compute Heat Rate ("CHR") framework estimates the electricity price at which different
AI workloads become economically indifferent between continuing to operate and curtailing.2 For
Q3 2026, the framework estimates a blended dispatch Compute Heat Rate ("CHR-D") of
approximately $9,071/MWh,           substantially   above     the   proposed   LLDMS      offer   ceiling
of $5,000/MWh. More significantly, workload categories representing approximately 76 percent
of the Index' s estimated electricity consumption have dispatch thresholds above $5,000/MWh,
including frontier inference at approximately $18,378/MWh, general-purpose inference at
approximately      $11,634/MWh,         and   enterprise    contracted   workloads   at   approximately
$8,104/MWh. While these values are modeled reference estimates rather than observed market
bids, they illustrate the fundamental economic challenge facing LLDMS: for much of the data
center sector, the opportunity cost of shutting down computing operations may exceed even the
maximum compensation available under the proposed service.
        Accordingly, for many large loads, the most viable pathway to provide meaningful grid
flexibility is not curtailment of the underlying facility, but rather private investment in co-located
generation and storage capable of dispatching on the customer' s behalf. A data center may be
unwilling or unable to shut down computing operations during an emergency, but it may be willing
to invest substantial private capital in generation and storage that allows the facility to continue
operating while rapidly reducing its reliance on the grid. The market framework should seek to
capture that capability rather than requiring customers to choose between continuity of operations
and providing reliability value to the ERCOT system.
        For this reason, ERock encourages the Commission and ERCOT to consider LLDMS as
only one component of the broader large load reliability framework and to prioritize development
of ERCOT' s Netted Network concept as part of the Batch 1+ process, with the goal of developing
and implementing the construct as early as practicable.

        Recent discussion at ERCOT's Large Load Working Group identified several limitations
of the existing Private Use Network ("PUN") and Withdrawal Limited PUN ("WLPUN')
frameworks. Under the existing construct, ERCOT' s market and Reliability Unit Commitment
("RUC") processes generally see only a site's net position, and therefore cannot fully utilize the
capability of generation and storage located behind a point of interconnection. The existing
framework can also significantly restrict the ability of co-located batteries and generation to
participate in ERCOT markets.
       ERCOT described the Netted Network concept as an operational and registration construct
that could provide greater visibility and control to ERCOT, greater operational flexibility to market
participants, and a better pathway for customers to monetize their assets. Under the Netted
Network concept, registered generation and storage resources' full capability would be visible to
ERCOT, allowing them to participate more fully in the market, rather than being limited to the
surplus remaining after serving native load.
       This opportunity is becoming increasingly important as large load customers deploy
significant amounts of onsite storage and generation for voltage ride through, load balancing,
resiliency, and other operational needs. During the LLWG discussion, stakeholders emphasized
that significant quantities of storage may be installed at data center facilities regardless of market
participation and urged ERCOT to develop a framework that captures the reliability value ofthose
assets rather than leaving substantial capability unavailable to ERCOT operations and markets.
ERCOT confirmed that obtaining greater operator visibility into co-located facilities was one of
the original motivations for the Netted Network concept.
       Batch Zero established important initial pathways through PCLR and WLPUN, but those
constructs remain limited. In Batch Zero, large load customers must choose between the PCLR
and WLPUN pathways rather than combining the capabilities of flexible load and co-located
resources. ERCOT specifically identified this limitation during the recent LLWG discussion and
raised the possibility of enabling greater integration of these concepts in future Batches.
       ERock therefore encourages the Commission to support and ERCOT to prioritize
development of the Netted Network construct through its Batch 1+ stakeholder process. LLDMS
may provide an additional emergency reliability tool, but it should not be viewed as the primary
mechanism for unlocking large load flexibility. A durable market framework that allows large
customers to maintain their core operations while making flexible demand, generation, and storage

                                             Page 3 of 5
 fully visible and available to ERCOT is more likely to attract private investment, provide
meaningful dispatchable reliability value, and create a sustainable model for integrating Texas's
rapidly growing large load sector.


CONCLUSION
        ERock appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments regarding the PFP for new
§25.521. As the Commission continues to move forward with Project No. 58482 and related
efforts, ERock is committed to supporting the effort to ensure improved grid reliability, resiliency,
and stability.



                                              Respectfully submitted,

                                              /s/ Monica Batra-Shrader
                                              Monica Batra-Shrader
                                              Policy Manager, Central Region

                           EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
The proposed as-needed procurement construct does not provide the certainty necessary
to support meaningful participation or investment.
For much of the data center sector, the opportunity cost of shutting down computing
operations may exceed the maximum compensation available under the proposed service.
The Commission and ERCOT should consider LLDMS as only one component of the
broader large load reliability framework and prioritize development of ERCOT' s Netted
Network concept as part of the Batch 1+ process, with the goal of developing and
implementing the construct as early as practicable.
LLDMS may provide an additional emergency reliability tool, but it should not be
viewed as the primary mechanism for unlocking large load flexibility.
A durable market framework that allows large customers to maintain their core
operations while making flexible demand, generation, and storage fully visible and
available to ERCOT is more likely to attract private investment, provide meaningful
dispatchable reliability value, and create a sustainable model for integrating Texas' s
rapidly growing large load sector.
